steps.user_message: I need help with my 2023 tax return. I'm head of household in Chicago IL. My W-2 from Riverside Hospital shows $64,800. I had $12,500 in 1099 income (marketing, 6 clients), $1,560 from Citi savings, and $290 from TD Ameritrade. I have a home office (130 sq ft, exclusive use); rent is $1,720/month for 620 sq ft total. Student loan interest: $4,100 (Navient, 2017–2019). I donated $1,350 to Habitat for Humanity with receipt, and had $1,350 in work expenses. What can I deduct, and should I itemize or take the standard deduction? What forms do I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Thanks — this is enough to give a clear, practical recommendation and an approximate tax impact. I’ll state assumptions I make and list what I need if you want a more precise calculation or return preparation.

Quick summary / recommendation
- You should report the $12,500 of 1099 (self‑employed) income on Schedule C. Those business expenses (the home‑office portion of your rent and the $1,350 of marketing/work expenses) reduce that business income and also reduce your self‑employment tax.
- The home‑office deduction can be taken (you qualify if the 130 sq ft is used exclusively and regularly for the business). You can use the actual‑expense method (Form 8829) or the simplified method ($5 × 130 sq ft = $650). Using the actual rent share looks far better from the numbers you gave.
- Student loan interest is an “above‑the‑line” deduction (up to $2,500, subject to a MAGI phaseout). Based on the income numbers you supplied, you will be in the phaseout range for 2023, so you’ll get a partial deduction (I estimate roughly $1,880 — see calculation below).
- Your $1,350 charitable donation is deductible only if you itemize. Because the Head‑of‑Household standard deduction for 2023 is $20,800, it is almost certainly better for you to take the standard deduction (unless you have other large deductible items you haven’t mentioned — mortgage interest, big state/local taxes, big medical expenses, etc.).
- You must report your interest income (Citi + TD Ameritrade = $1,850). Because interest > $1,500, you’ll also file Schedule B.

Forms you will likely need (federal, 2023)
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (for adjustments such as student loan interest and the deduction for half of self‑employment tax)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report the 1099 income and business expenses
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax (and the half of SE tax that’s deductible)
- Form 8829 — if you use the actual home‑office method (if you use the simplified method you do not use Form 8829)
- Schedule B — because your interest income exceeds $1,500
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A — possible Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction (20% of qualified business income) — you may qualify; depends on taxable income level and whether your trade is a specified service. If taxable income is well under the phaseout threshold, you likely can claim up to 20% of your QBI.
- Schedule A — only if you choose to itemize (seems unlikely based on the info you gave)

Illinois state
- File IL‑1040. Illinois uses your federal AGI as a starting point (there are specific additions/subtractions at the state level). Illinois applies a flat tax rate (check the current rate on the IL Dept. of Revenue website; as of recent years it has been 4.95%).

Estimates / illustrative calculation (based on numbers you gave; round numbers)
I’ll show an approximate computation with the following assumptions:
- The $1,350 work expenses are legitimate business expenses related to your 1099 marketing income.
- You use the actual home‑office method and take the rent share as a business expense.
Calculations:
- W‑2 wages: 64,800
- 1099 self‑employment gross: 12,500
- Interest income: 1,560 + 290 = 1,850
- Total gross income = 64,800 + 12,500 + 1,850 = 79,150

Home office portion of rent:
- Home size = 620 sq ft; office = 130 sq ft → office = 130/620 ≈ 20.97%
- Annual rent = $1,720 × 12 = $20,640
- Office portion of rent ≈ $20,640 × 0.2097 ≈ $4,333

Business expenses (assumed):
- Home‑office portion of rent ≈ $4,333
- Other business (marketing) expenses = $1,350
- Total business expenses ≈ $5,683

Net self‑employment profit:
- 12,500 − 5,683 ≈ $6,817

Self‑employment tax (approx):
- Net earnings for SE tax = 6,817 × 0.9235 ≈ 6,295
- SE tax ≈ 6,295 × 15.3% ≈ $962
- Half of SE tax deductible above the line ≈ $481

MAGI for student loan phaseout (rough):
- Gross 79,150 − half SE tax 481 ≈ $78,669
- Phaseout for student loan interest for single/HOH in 2023 is $75,000–$90,000, so you are in the phaseout range.
- Maximum deduction is $2,500. Reduction ≈ 2,500 × (78,669 − 75,000) / 15,000 ≈ $612
- Estimated allowable student loan interest deduction ≈ 2,500 − 612 ≈ $1,888 (cannot exceed interest actually paid; you reported $4,100 so this is fine)

Taxable income estimate (very rough):
- AGI after student loan interest ≈ 78,669 − 1,888 ≈ 76,781
- Subtract Head‑of‑Household standard deduction 20,800 → taxable income ≈ $55,981

Income tax (very rough) + SE tax:
- Federal income tax on ~$55,981 (HOH 2023 brackets) ≈ $6,433
- Plus SE tax ≈ $962
- Total federal tax ≈ $7,395 (credits, withholdings, QBI deduction, and exact rounding can change this).

Key things I need you to confirm (or provide) to refine calculations
1. Are the $1,350 of “work expenses” business expenses related to the 1099 marketing work, or are they unreimbursed employee expenses related to your W‑2 job? (If the latter, they are not deductible for 2018–2025.)
2. Is the 130 sq ft home office used exclusively for the 1099 business? Do you want to use the actual expense method (larger deduction, needs Form 8829) or the simplified method ($5 × sq ft = $650)?
3. Did you actually pay $4,100 of student loan interest in 2023? (Student loan interest deduction is for interest you paid in the tax year; lenders typically issue Form 1098‑E if > $600 — do you have a 1098‑E for 2023?)
4. Any other deductible items not mentioned: mortgage interest, property tax, large state taxes, large medical expenses, retirement contributions (IRA, SEP/solo‑401(k)), or any estimated tax payments made?
5. Do you want me to compute a more precise federal tax estimate including QBI and exact tax bracket calculations, or an Illinois state estimate?

Next steps I can take for you
- If you confirm answers to the questions above I can run a more precise tax estimate (showing alternate results for simplified vs actual home office method and with/without QBI).
- I can prepare a checklist of documents for your tax preparer or for e‑filing.
- I can draft an email to your tax preparer with these numbers and questions (if you want me to send or draft that).

Would you like me to run a precise estimate and include the QBI deduction? If so, please confirm items (1)–(3) above and tell me whether you want the actual or simplified home‑office method.
